structure.title: 5.1 Main results (bunching, missing mass, conditional disparity)
5.3 The impact of Alleyne v. United States

observations.statement: The empirical strategy is named as the difference-in-bunching method following Kleven; the estimand is the change in the probability a case falls in a narrow bin just above the new threshold, comparing post-reform to pre-reform distributions. The counterfactual assumption (pre-2010 distribution as counterfactual for post-2010) is stated explicitly.
observations.quote: the pre-2010 distribution is a good counterfactual

observations.statement: A second, separately stated assumption is used for the conditional racial disparity: the pre-2010 distribution above the old threshold reflects true drug involvement. The author spells out how each direction of possible bias in pre-2010 charged amounts would change the interpretation of equal distributions by race.

For the Supreme Court decision, the author explains why the bunching counterfactual is not credible in that window and switches to a difference-in-discontinuities design in time, comparing the jump at the decision date to jumps at the same calendar date in other years, under a stated continuity assumption on case characteristics.
observations.quote: relies on the weaker assumption that case characteristics are continuous

observations.statement: The discrimination analysis is explicitly classified as a benchmark test and the two assumptions under which such tests identify taste-based bias (from Canay, Mogstad and Mountjoy) are stated up front, with a caveat that bias is identified only if they hold.

A conceptual framework of prosecutor objectives yields directional predictions for each segment of the quantity distribution after the threshold change; these predictions are later placed as a row in the missing-mass table and tested against estimates.

Main data are USSC sentencing records for federal drug cases over a stated multi-year window; the unit is the sentenced case, restricted to crack-cocaine offenses because that is the only drug whose threshold changes over time.

Exclusions are listed and justified: cases with missing or range-coded drug weights, cases flagged for data problems, cases where the court changed or rejected the findings of fact, and a top trim on drug weight to remove outliers; the author notes that the share excluded does not jump at the reform and that including range-coded cases strengthens the result.

Several auxiliary datasets from different stages of the criminal process are introduced with their purpose: state inmate records, two drug seizure systems, a national drug use survey, EOUSA prosecutor case-management files, and a state-level Google Trends animus measure. A timeline figure in the appendix maps each dataset to a process stage.

Because prosecutor files lack race, defendant race is imputed from the racial composition of USSC sentencing in each district-year-month; seizure quantities are linked to USSC cases at the state-by-month level with lags to allow for the gap between arrest and sentencing.
Observation counts are reported in every regression table, including by column when the sample changes, and summary statistics report counts by period.

The outcome is a binary indicator that the recorded drug amount falls in a narrow ten-gram bin at and above the new threshold; the treatment indicator is sentencing under post-reform Guidelines amendment years. Race is collapsed into a black-or-Hispanic indicator, with a footnote acknowledging the crudeness and stating that splitting the groups gives similar results.

Missing mass is examined by re-estimating the same model with the dependent variable redefined over a list of adjacent quantity ranges spanning the distribution, plus two broad ranges below and above the threshold.

Prosecutors are classified as bunching or non-bunching by comparing the share of their post-reform cases in the bunching bin to the pre-reform baseline share, using a leave-out mean to avoid a mechanical relation, and restricting to attorneys with a minimum caseload; a second definition uses bunching at the old threshold before the reform.

A predicted sentence is built by regressing sentence on offender characteristics in pre-reform data and applying the coefficients to post-reform cases, then split into quantiles; a case-complexity index for prosecutors is built from a regression of drug weight on case attributes and averaged over prior cases.

The main table has two columns, the pooled effect and the race-interacted version, with robust standard errors stated in the notes, a row giving the p-value for equality of the race-specific coefficients, and a pointer to appendix tables for robustness.

Missing-mass tables note that standard errors are estimated jointly across ranges by seemingly unrelated regression so that coefficients can be summed and compared; the race-specific version adds race-specific linear trends and district fixed effects, stated in the title and notes, and reports a sample-period row.

The heterogeneity table mixes standard error types by column: robust for offender-level splits and clustered at the state level for state-level splits, which the notes state explicitly; two p-value rows test race equality with and without the characteristic.

The Alleyne table reports the pooled discontinuity and the year-specific discontinuity across columns that vary only the bandwidth, with a bandwidth row and observation counts; the notes state clustering at the case-received date and the source of the optimal bandwidth.

Because the post-reform white subsample is small, the author runs a placebo exercise reassigning white offenders to the bunching bin at the minority rates and compares the actual disparity to the placebo distribution, reporting the exercise in an appendix figure.
Robust standard errors are used for the main specification without an explicit rationale in the text; alternative standard error methods are mentioned only as an appendix robustness item.

For prosecutor-level regressions, standard errors are clustered at the prosecutor level (the unit whose classification defines the regressor) and the notes report that bootstrapping to account for the estimated classification gives similar results; the share of bunching attorneys gets a stratified bootstrap standard error.

When many narrow-bin coefficients are individually noisy, the author reports a joint test over the contiguous range rather than relying on single bins, and states which bins are individually significant in the figure notes.

The paper checks that the pre-reform share of cases in the future bunching bin is stable near zero across years (supporting the counterfactual) and reports the density of cases around the Supreme Court decision date in an appendix figure.
Distributional equality by race in the pre-reform window is tested with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, shown as overlaid distributions in a main-text figure with the test result in the notes.

The time-discontinuity design reports an optimal bandwidth from Imbens and Kalyanaraman alongside wider and narrower bandwidths in the main table, and polynomial and further bandwidth choices in an appendix figure; a very narrow window is used to separate the court decision from a later policy memo.
Placebo dates are checked: no change at the certiorari announcement or oral argument dates, and no change when the related memo is later rescinded, reported in a footnote and an appendix table.
For the sentencing discontinuity, a predicted-sentence version of the RD plot is shown to check for selection at the threshold, and the design is re-run on states with little bunching.

Main-result robustness is summarised in one paragraph listing sample restrictions, state fixed effects and trends, offender controls, nonlinear estimators, wider bunching bins, inclusion of range-coded cases, and alternative standard errors, with all tables in the appendix; the share of the disparity surviving finer fixed effects is described in words.

The missing-mass analysis is repeated with a later start year to address secular trends around a prior Supreme Court case, shown as additional columns of the same main-text table, and on trial cases only, reported inline with coefficients and standard errors in the text.

Prosecutor-level results are checked against alternative minimum caseload cutoffs and against imputing missing quantities as zero, with the author calling the caseload cutoff a necessarily arbitrary restriction.
observations.locator: footnotes 13 and 14, Table A9, Table A10

observations.statement: The animus result is probed in an appendix table by adding individual and district controls interacted with post-by-race, using the continuous animus measure, and substituting an occupation-specific implicit association measure with state-by-post-by-race fixed effects.

Heterogeneity is estimated by fully interacting the race model with binary offender or district characteristics, one per column, and used as a test that race is not a proxy for those characteristics; narrower splits by criminal history and predicted-sentence quantiles are shown graphically with within-group tests in the notes.

Bunching is estimated separately for each lead attorney, and the share of attorneys responsible is quantified; the labels are validated with an empirical-null false discovery rate procedure and a Bayesian shrinkage deconvolution, each with a named source.

Alternative channels (offender behaviour, state-to-federal case shifting, law enforcement tactics) are each ruled out with a dataset from the corresponding stage of the process before turning to prosecutors, and the absence of bunching in seizure records is used to locate discretion at the prosecutor stage.

Persistence of prosecutor bunching across districts, thresholds and time, and spillovers to colleagues after a bunching attorney moves, are used to argue the metric captures prosecutor type; the spillover evidence is labelled highly suggestive.
observations.locator: Section 5.2.5, Tables A11 and A12, Figure A10

observations.statement: Statistical versus taste-based discrimination is discussed through a simple model whose implications are checked against within-district prosecutor variation and prosecutor experience measures; the animus correlation is presented as suggestive evidence of taste-based bias.

Cost-based explanations are addressed by splitting districts on private counsel retention, on shares of cases declined for weak evidence or resources, and by checking that judges, unlike prosecutors, do not bunch consistently across thresholds.

Effect sizes are interpreted as ratios of the race-specific coefficients and as the share of the excess mass accounted for by the missing mass below the threshold, with a confidence interval on that share; imprecision for the small white subsample is discussed explicitly.

A back-of-envelope exercise converts sentencing effects into sentence-years and dollar costs using a per-year incarceration cost from cited studies, applies the bunching rates to all federal drug cases under an explicitly conservative assumption, and reports alternative assumptions in an appendix table.
A prior study is reconciled in a footnote by replicating its result on its fiscal years and attributing the difference to changes in the Guidelines structure.

The author states that the missing mass cannot be shown with certainty to be where excess-mass cases would have been recorded, that trial status is endogenous, and that case assignment to prosecutors is not random.
Limitations of the prosecutor files are stated: no race field, many missing quantities, and small caseloads per attorney that prevent identifying bad behaviour by individuals.

The paper clarifies it is not an evaluation of the reform, that the results do not imply discretion began after the reform, and that taste-based bias is identified only under the benchmark-test assumptions.

Figures begin with raw density histograms of drug amounts pre and post reform and a yearly share plot by race; tables use three-level significance stars, and notes state the data source, standard error type, the estimating equation, and pointers to appendix variants. A summary statistics table by period opens the data section.

Later figures include a coefficient plot of bin-by-bin race differences scaled by bin share, RD-style binned plots of sentence against drug amount with linear fits on each side, and event-study plots for the FSA; the figure notes carry the estimating equations and key statistics.
Appendix tables and figures are numbered with an A prefix and referenced heavily; a table row labelled 'Predicted change' juxtaposes theory predictions with estimates.

The introduction previews all main findings and the sequence of supporting results, followed by a related-literature subsection with numbered contributions; the paper then goes background, data, methodology, results, conclusion. Robustness is a named subsection heading within the main results rather than a separate section, with details in the appendix.

Results open with the headline bunching estimate and its robustness, then progress through missing mass, conditional disparity, prosecutor discretion, the court decision, discrimination mechanisms, and finally sentencing impacts and cost estimates. Methodology for later sections is deferred to those sections rather than the methods section.
A data availability statement gives a Zenodo DOI for the data and code; supplementary material is said to be available online. No software is named in the text.

Data are public administrative releases (USSC, EOUSA case files, state inmate records, seizure systems) and national surveys, combined with a published state-level index; no restricted-access procedure is described.

The author argues the setting is chosen for identification but notes bunching disparities appear for other drugs and that bunching attorneys bunch at other thresholds, and uses this to justify extrapolating to all federal drug cases in the cost exercise.

Net effects of the reform are estimated with a difference-in-differences event study comparing crack-cocaine cases to other drug cases, restricted to post-Kimbrough years, with parallel trends stated as the assumption in the figure notes.

gaps: No explicit justification for using robust (unclustered) standard errors in the main specification.
No software or package named in the text; only a Zenodo DOI for data and code.
No preregistration, IRB or ethics statement.
Online appendix (Tables A1 to A21, Figures A1 to A12) is not included in the text file; appendix content is known only through in-text references.
No multiple testing adjustment discussed for the many heterogeneity columns.
